draft.title: Plant responses to pathogens
card: Physical barriers
Plants have structures that keep pathogens out. These include a waxy cuticle on leaves, thick cell walls and bark on woody stems.
Chemical defences
Plants make chemicals that harm pathogens, such as antimicrobial compounds and enzymes that break down fungal cell walls. Some are always present. Others are made after an infection starts.
Cell death
A plant can kill its own cells around the infection site. The pathogen is left without living cells to feed on, so it cannot spread further. This is called the hypersensitive response.
Plants have no antibodies and no mobile immune cells. Their defences work in the cells and tissues where the pathogen arrives.
draft.remember: Plants block pathogens, poison them, and sacrifice infected cells to stop the spread.

a.q: A fungus enters a leaf. The plant kills the cells around the entry point, and the fungus cannot spread past them. Why does this stop the fungus?
opts: The fungus has no living cells to feed on
The dead cells release antibodies that attack it
The dead cells make a thicker waxy cuticle
Mobile immune cells then engulf the fungus
a.why: The fungus needs living cells to feed on. Killing the cells around the infection takes that away, so the pathogen is contained. Plants have no antibodies or mobile immune cells, so the options that rely on them are wrong.
a.clue: Think about what the pathogen needs from living cells.

b.q: A scientist compares two wheat plants infected by the same fungus. Plant X makes antimicrobial compounds in its leaves. Plant Y has a thicker cuticle. Which type of defence does each plant show?
opts: X is a chemical defence and Y is a physical barrier
X is a physical barrier and Y is a chemical defence
Both are physical barriers
X is a chemical defence and Y is cell death
b.why: Antimicrobial compounds are chemicals that harm pathogens, so X shows a chemical defence. A thicker cuticle is a structure that keeps pathogens out, so Y shows a physical barrier. Cell death means the plant kills its own cells, which Y's cuticle does not do.
b.clue: Ask whether each defence is a substance or a structure.

a.best: The fungus has no living cells to feed on

b.best: X is a chemical defence and Y is a physical barrier

problems.detail: 'Their defences work in the cells and tissues where the pathogen arrives' oversimplifies. Plants also have systemic acquired resistance, in which signals such as salicylic acid spread from the infection site and prime defences across the whole plant. The line could teach that plant defences are only ever local.
The clue 'Think about what the pathogen needs from living cells' points straight at the only option about living cells, so it nearly gives the answer away.
